1.title: Know the words and the kinds of driving work
1.intro: Ride and delivery driving means moving people or goods for pay through an app or a company. Start with the basics.
pts: Learn the terms: trip, fare, tip, surge, fee, shift, route, active time, self-employed.
Kinds of work: rides, food delivery, parcel delivery, courier.
Most app drivers are paid per trip and pay their own costs.
Name the hours and zones with the most demand near you.
Read how the app calculates fares and what share you keep.
List what you need to start: licence, vehicle, phone, insurance and account approval.
Compare delivery by car, bike and on foot where allowed, and say which suits you.
1.ex: Lunch hours in a business area have many short delivery trips; late nights near venues have more rides. If a lunch hour gives 4 trips at 5 dollars each, 4 x 5 = 20 dollars before costs.
1.act: Write a table of work type, pay style, vehicle and hours for three kinds of driving.
1.std: Task: compare three kinds of work. Condition: from public information. Standard: table complete and accurate.

2.title: Explain a driving shift from start to end
2.intro: A shift has steps. If you can name them, you plan time, fuel and safety.
pts: The steps: vehicle check, go online, accept trips, pickup, drop-off, break, go offline, log.
Check tyres, lights, brakes, fluids and cleanliness before you start.
Plan breaks and rest; tired driving is dangerous.
Record start and end time, kilometres and earnings every shift.
Set a stop time before you start and keep to it.
Keep water, a phone charger and a first aid kit in the vehicle.
Write down each trip's start and end place so you can review the day.
2.ex: Before a shift you check tyres and lights, charge your phone, and plan a rest at the fourth hour. An 8-hour shift with a 30-minute break gives 8 - 0.5 = 7.5 hours of driving time.
2.act: Build a pre-shift checklist and a shift log.
2.std: Task: make two forms. Condition: one page each. Standard: all checks present and usable on a real shift.

3.title: Drive safely and serve people well
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Drive safely and treat customers with care.
pts: Follow all traffic laws; never use a hand-held phone while driving.
Keep a calm voice, confirm the pickup and say the destination.
Keep the car clean and handle food or parcels with care.
Report any problem with a trip through the app support.
Park legally and never block traffic, hydrants or bike lanes.
Offer help with bags only when it is safe and agreed.
Decide in advance what you do if a trip feels unsafe: refuse or end it, and report.
3.ex: A rider is not at the pickup. You wait the allowed time, call, and then follow the app's no-show steps. If the allowed wait is 5 minutes and you arrived at 6:10, you may leave at 6:15.
3.act: Role-play ten pickups with a friend and write what you would change.
3.std: Task: practise ten trips. Condition: parked, with a friend as customer. Standard: greeting, confirmation and handover done every time.

4.title: Follow Canadian rules for drivers
4.intro: Rules for driving for pay differ by province and city. Learn which ones touch you.
pts: You need the right licence class for your vehicle; some places need extra checks or permits for ride work. Check the current rule with the provincial transport office.
Ordinary personal insurance may not cover paid driving; ask your insurer what cover you need.
Cities can set rules for taxis and ride services; check the current rule with the local authority.
App drivers are usually self-employed; income is taxable and sales tax rules may apply. Check with the tax agency.
Ask whether your vehicle must pass an inspection for this work; check the provincial rule.
Ask the provincial transport office whether your vehicle needs any special plates or permits for paid driving.
Keep your licence, registration and insurance papers current and in the vehicle.
4.ex: You ask your insurer in writing: 'Am I covered when I drive for a ride app?' and keep the reply. If the reply says you need extra cover, you buy it before your next shift. You file the reply with your insurance papers.
4.act: Build a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten items.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unknowns say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Work out real earnings
5.intro: Your pay is what is left after vehicle costs. Work the numbers.
pts: Costs: fuel or charging, insurance, repairs, tyres, depreciation, phone, parking and fees.
Cost per kilometre = yearly vehicle costs / yearly kilometres.
Real hourly pay = (earnings - costs) / total hours, including waiting.
Plan for slow weeks by keeping a small cash buffer.
Count unpaid time: waiting, driving to a pickup and charging.
Spread large costs, such as tyres, over the kilometres they last.
Set aside an amount for tax from every payout.
5.ex: Earnings 154, fuel and wear 42, hours 7: net = 154 - 42 = 112, and real pay = 112 / 7 = 16 per hour. If yearly vehicle costs are 6,000 and you drive 20,000 km, cost = 6,000 / 20,000 = 0.30 per km. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Log five shifts and compute real pay per hour for each.
5.std: Task: compute real pay. Condition: from your own log. Standard: all costs shown and a mentor can follow.

6.title: Find the best times and keep a good record
6.intro: Better planning raises pay and lowers risk. Use your log to decide.
pts: Compare pay per hour by day and time of day.
Avoid long unpaid waits and trips that end far from demand.
Keep ratings steady by being on time and polite.
Keep receipts and a mileage log for tax.
Mark the zones where you wait longest and test a different zone.
Compare whole weeks, not single days, before you change your hours.
Note weather and events that change demand.
6.ex: Your log shows Friday lunch pays 20 per hour and Tuesday afternoon 11. Working 4 hours of Friday lunch instead of Tuesday afternoon earns 4 x 20 - 4 x 11 = 36 more. You work more Friday lunch.
6.act: Compare ten shifts and write a plan for next month.
6.std: Task: analyse ten shifts. Condition: with simple spreadsheet. Standard: the plan uses numbers.

7.title: Protect yourself, your passengers and your data
7.intro: Safe habits protect you, others and your account.
pts: Wear a seat belt, rest when tired and never drive after alcohol or drugs.
Know the emergency steps: pull over safely, call emergency services, report in the app.
Keep customer addresses private.
Know how to stay safe at night and in unknown places.
Share your trip with a trusted person when working at night, if the app allows.
Check the provincial rule before you record passengers with a camera.
Plan for a breakdown: safe stopping place, tow number and warning lights.
7.ex: A customer is rude. You stay calm, end the trip at a safe place and report it to the app. You write the time and place in your log so you can show what happened.
7.act: Write an emergency card, a pre-trip check and a privacy note.
7.std: Task: write three documents. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each is clear and ready to use.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Drive, measure and decide whether it is worth it.
pts: Set a 60-day goal, such as 60 hours and a real hourly pay target.
Every week record hours, kilometres, income, costs and safety events.
Ask: do I earn enough after costs and tax?
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
Compare real pay with your pay target after costs and tax.
List the hours you will stop working.
Check your vehicle's condition and costs after 60 days.
8.ex: After 60 days: 62 hours, real pay 16 per hour, no incidents. Total real pay = 62 x 16 = 992. You decide to drive only the best 20 hours a week.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: legal, insured driving. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What does self-employed mean for an app driver?
You pay your own costs and taxes.
What do you check before a shift?
Tyres, lights, brakes, fluids and cleanliness.
Is a hand-held phone allowed while driving?
No.
What should you ask your insurer?
Whether personal insurance covers paid driving.
How do you find real hourly pay?
Earnings minus costs, divided by all hours including waiting.
Name three vehicle costs.
Fuel, insurance, repairs, tyres or depreciation.
Why keep a mileage log?
For tax and to measure cost per kilometre.
What do you do if you are tired?
Stop and rest.
Who sets taxi and ride rules?
Provinces and cities; check the current rule with the local authority.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
